strengths: Clear problem motivation with compelling empirical evidence (Figure 1) that token order significantly affects AR-based classification outcomes

Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple baseline families, OOD benchmarks, and real-world distribution shifts with thorough ablations (likelihood strategies, tokenizers, per-token analysis)

Strong empirical results: outperforms diffusion classifiers, achieves competitive performance with DINOv2, and demonstrates significant efficiency gains (25× faster), representing first GC approach competitive with state-of-the-art SSL
Excellent analysis and visualization of order effects through per-token likelihood heatmaps and prefix length studies, providing intuitive understanding of why marginalization improves performance
Fair experimental design with consistent model architectures, resolutions, and sizes across baselines; proper handling of methods without public checkpoints through careful re-implementation
Technically sound use of Jensen's inequality for deriving order-unconditional likelihood lower bound with reasonable hypothesis for why it outperforms direct likelihood estimation
Strong reproducibility: detailed appendices with hyperparameters, model settings, and promise of code/model release
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty: the core contribution is applying existing RandAR model with straightforward ensemble averaging over permutations—no new architecture, objective, or tokenization scheme introduced

Incomplete theoretical understanding of why order marginalization improves classification; lacks rigorous analysis of order complementarity, conditions enabling improvement, and what different orders capture
Heavy dependence on RandAR's specific architecture with position encodings; limited exploration of generalization to other any-order AR models or whether insights are broadly applicable

Computational cost scaling with number of classes not adequately addressed: K×M forward passes (K orders, M classes) becomes prohibitive for large-class problems; efficiency advantage overstated given this linear scaling

Order selection (K=20) appears arbitrary, matching diffusion timesteps without principled justification; insufficient analysis of benefit saturation or optimal K selection across computational budgets
Competitive but not dominant over DINOv2: RandAR-XL trails by 1.4% on IN-Val (81.3% vs 82.7%) and significantly on IN-A (23.3% vs 36.3%), somewhat weakening 'competitive performance' claims

Tokenizer sensitivity: different VQ-VAE tokenizers show material performance differences; latent noise augmentation required for LlamaGen but not MaskGIT suggests potential brittleness; WILDS experiments use different tokenizer than main experiments (inconsistency)
Evaluation limited to 256×256 resolution and image classification; no investigation of higher resolutions, other visual domains, or transfer learning scenarios; timing breakdown not provided
Limited exploration of whether orders capture complementary information; no investigation of structured vs. random order sampling strategies or connection between order structure and performance
Class token interaction with position instructions and permutations insufficiently explained; RandAR training from scratch without exploration of transfer learning or pretrained variants

strengths: Comprehensive experimental validation across multiple benchmarks (ImageNet variants, WILDS distribution shifts, ObjectNet, COCO) with consistent experimental protocols demonstrating clear improvements over diffusion classifiers and competitive performance with DINOv2

Clear and well-motivated insight identifying token order as an important inductive bias in AR classifiers, with compelling visualizations (Figure 1) and thorough interpretability analysis (per-token likelihoods, per-token accuracy) explaining how order marginalization works
Significant efficiency gains: 25× faster than DiT while maintaining superior accuracy across most benchmarks, addressing a practical limitation of generative classifiers

Particularly strong out-of-distribution robustness, outperforming both diffusion-based and discriminative baselines on multiple OOD sets, plus superior performance on WILDS distribution shift benchmarks

Thorough ablations and analysis including VQ-VAE tokenizer comparison with noise robustness analysis, likelihood estimation strategy validation, generalization beyond RandAR, and proper formalization of connection to masked diffusion
First comparative study of generative classifiers against state-of-the-art self-supervised methods (DINOv2), providing valuable perspective on generative vs discriminative approaches

Technical soundness with proper mathematical derivations, fair comparisons using consistent architectures/resolutions/token counts, and reproducibility through promised code release and detailed implementation specifications
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: the core contribution is a straightforward application of order ensembling to an existing model (RandAR), lacking novel algorithmic insights or theoretical advances beyond identifying that averaging over orders helps

Strong architectural dependency: method requires RandAR, one of few any-order AR models; generalization demonstrated only with RAR-B; severely restricts applicability and impact, requiring practitioners to wait for compatible models

Incomplete theoretical understanding of why order marginalization helps beyond ensemble averaging—lacks principled analysis of whether benefits stem from coverage, voting mechanisms, or deeper structural properties of random image token orders

Notable performance gap with DINOv2: 1.4% lower on ImageNet-Val (81.3% vs 82.7%), significantly lower on IN-A (23.3% vs 36.3%), and DINOv2 trained on more data (ImageNet-21K+1K vs 1K only), complicating fair comparison

Unjustified choice of likelihood lower bound (Eq. 5) over direct likelihood estimate: explanation that 'RandAR was trained on Eq. 5' is post-hoc rationalization; raises questions about whether models optimize for intended objectives versus observed training procedure

Significant tokenization dependency: performance varies with VQ-VAE choice (1-2% differences), latent noise augmentation required only for LlamaGen, and unclear why design is not robust across tokenizers; introduces additional moving parts affecting results

Limited generalization evaluation: primarily natural image classification; noticeably worse performance on ObjectNet/COCO than DINOv2; no evaluation on other domains (medical, satellite, documents); noise augmentation appears dataset-dependent

Computational cost remains problematic: despite 25× speedup, still requires K=20 passes per image, resulting in 20,000+ inferences for 1000-class problems—impractical compared to single-pass discriminative models; paper acknowledges but doesn't adequately address
